newsitem.title: TURKEY: Volatility in US treasuries delays Turk Eurobond.
newsitem.headline: Volatility in US treasuries delays Turk Eurobond.

text.p: Increased volatility in the U.S. Treasury market has delayed Turkey's five-year dollar eurobond issue, which had been expected last week, government officials said on Thursday.

"The volatility in international capital and U.S Treasury market created uncertainties in pricing. Therefore we decided to launch bonds when we see stability in these markets," said a government official who declined to be named.

Turkey was initially expected to launch its $250 million Eurobonds, underwritten by JP Morgan and SBC Warburg, last week, following roadshows in key financial centres in Europe, Asia and the United States earlier this month.
The official did not say when the issue would be launched.
Officials say increased political uncertainty which sent Turkish shares plunging on Thursday has not played any role in the decision to delay the Euro issue.
Istanbul shares fell 4.9 percent on Thursday over press reports that Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's coalition government may collapse.
Bankers say the appetite for emerging market instruments had fallen sharply after the volatility in the U.S market and expectations for a rate hike by the Federal Reserve (Fed) increased.
The Fed's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will meet on May 20 when the Fed, some bankers believe, would increase rates.
Bankers say some other emerging market countries -- the Philippines, Hungary and Russia, have also delayed their Eurodollar issue plans on weak market conditions.

Turkey had issued 300 billion lira of five-year and 500 million marks of seven year Eurobonds earlier this year, taking advantage of favourable market conditions despite its speculative credit ratings from leading agencies.
It has a B rating from Standard and Poor's and B1 from Moody's.
The country, which services around $7.5 billion of external debt a year, is planning to raise at least $2 billion from international capital markets this year.
It finances the gap through project loans and domestic borrowing at very high real rates.
